quotes.t: You told me some days ago what Lorenzo dei Medici discussed with you concerning being and the one. Supported by the reasons of the Platonists, he disputed against Aristotle, on whose Ethics you are giving a public commentary this year.

open.t: The text names no individual Platonist behind the 'reasons of the Platonists' Lorenzo used; whether these were drawn from Ficino is not stated here.

bears.note: Lorenzo is the Platonists' advocate in the discussion that occasions the treatise.

judged.justification: Fixes the occasion: a Medici-circle dispute on Plato against Aristotle, not an attack on a named Platonist.

quotes.t: And since those who think that Aristotle disagrees with Plato disagree with me, who make a concordant philosophy of both, you asked both how Aristotle might be defended in this matter and also how he might agree with his master, …

bears.note: Poliziano put the question of how Aristotle might agree with Plato.

judged.justification: States the concordist purpose that governs the whole argument.

quotes.t: I said what came to my mind at that time, confirming what you answered to Lorenzo in the discussion rather than bringing in anything new.

open.t: The proem does not say what Poliziano answered to Lorenzo, so which arguments of the treatise are Poliziano's and which Pico's cannot be told from the text.

quotes.t: Although I am to write at greater length on these topics in the Concord of Plato and Aristotle which I am now bringing forth, you entreated me to collect in a brief compendium what I said about this question then …

bears.note: Pico's own words on his closeness to Poliziano.

quotes.t: Aristotle says in many places that the one and being, and likewise the true and the good, correspond to each other and are the same in extent.
We shall treat of the true and the good later. The Academy opposes this, and thinks that the one is prior to being.

open.t: The Academy is not identified by any author's name in this chapter.

judged.justification: Sets out the two positions whose reconciliation the treatise attempts.

quotes.t: I find that Plato disputed concerning being and the one in two places, namely, in the Parmenides and the Sophist. The Academics contend that in both passages Plato places the one above being.

warrants.t: The argument from the construction of the dialogue: where it begins, what it tends to, what it promises and what it asserts.

open.t: The chapter does not say which interpreters hold the Parmenides to teach a doctrine of the one; the author omits them by name.

judged.justification: Denies the Parmenides doctrinal status on which the Neoplatonic one-beyond-being rests, so a central text is read as method.

open.t: The persons whose commentaries are called arbitrary and forced are not named in the text, so the quotation does not identify the target.

judged.justification: The sharpest polemic in the treatise is not addressed to a name; its target must be supplied from outside the text.

warrants.t: An argument from what Zeno says of who may properly exhibit the exercise, and of the unsuitability of first principles as a topic of shame.

quotes.t: Notice also (if this be not a dialectical exercise but conveys a doctrine concerning being and the one), how much these two differ, that is, to assert that the one is above being, and to assert this as future: that, …

warrants.t: The hypothesis is conditional, so it cannot be a categorical statement of the one's transcendence even if the dialogue is doctrinal.

judged.justification: Gives a second, independent reading of the first hypothesis that does not depend on the dialectical-exercise thesis.

quotes.t: So much for Plato. Consequently, according to him, not-one and nothing are equals, indeed, they are the same. One and something are equals.
It appears, then, that Plato held it as certain that the one was being.

But let this be so, let us grant that Plato affirmed something which he certainly nowhere affirmed. Well, let us examine in what sense Plato could have spoken truly, first laying down the foundations of the Aristotelean position in this …

judged.justification: The move from exegesis to metaphysical reconciliation: the concord no longer depends on winning the exegetical point.

quotes.t: This term being, about which it is argued whether it be equal to the one, can be taken in two modes.
we say being, we understand all that which is outside nothing. Aristotle employed the term in this way when he made being equal to the one.

judged.justification: A stated rule of speech that licenses reading Aristotle's usage as popular, not as the last word on God.

quotes.t: Parmenides the Pythagorean, when he said that that which is, is one, meant God, if we believe Simplicius and the many others who wish to defend Parmenides from those who calumniate him, as if he had said that all things …
This one is God. Therefore, if we believe Parmenides and even his Platonic defenders, the one cannot be above being, unless it is above God.

warrants.t: The author appeals to Simplicius and other defenders of Parmenides for the reading that the one is God.

quotes.t: But also Dionysius the Areopagite, whom those who dispute against us make into a patron of their opinion, will not deny that God truly said to Moses "I am who am," which we read thus in Greek

open.t: The 'opponents' who make Dionysius a patron of the one-above-being view are not named.

warrants.t: A reductio on the Platonists' third argument (ch. 1) applied to God.

judged.justification: The central convertibility argument in its first sense of being.

quotes.t: We have explained one of the two modes in which we said that being could be understood. Those who use being in this sense, as they can use it correctly, most truly affirm that nothing is more universal than being. …

judged.justification: Concedes to the Platonists, in a defined sense, what the first mode denied.

quotes.t: Some nouns are concrete, others abstract. Hot, shining, white, man, are concrete. Heat, light, whiteness, humanity, are abstract. Their meaning and difference is that what is called abstract signifies that which is such from itself and not from another. The …

Being has the aspect of a concrete noun. Being, and that which is, are the same in meaning. This word existence [esse] seems to be the abstract form of the preceding terms. That which participates existence [esse] is called being …

judged.justification: The ens/esse distinction is the engine of the whole reconciliation.

quotes.t: Therefore, if we should look at this exact signification of being, we shall deny being not only to what is not, and to what is nothing, but to that which is to such a degree that it is existence [ipsum …
For God, who is the plentitude of all existence, is of this nature. He alone is of himself, and from him alone, with no interposing medium, all things proceed to existence.
For this reason, we may truly say that God is not being, but is above being, and that something is higher than being

judged.justification: Grants the Platonists' formula 'God is above being' by a Thomist route (ipsum esse above ens), so the dispute over the one is redescribed as a dispute over the sense of 'being'.

quotes.t: God, and since the title one is given to God, we may consequently say that he is the one above being.

warrants.t: Pico invokes Dionysius, De divinis nominibus, for the two glosses on 'one'.

quotes.t: Consequently, if, as the Academics think, Plato affirms in the first hypothesis of the Parmenides that the one is higher than being, that one will be nothing other than God, as even the Academics admit. They assert by common consent …

judged.justification: Turns the Neoplatonists' one into a claim about God, then absorbs it into the ens/esse distinction.

quotes.t: Aristotle says in First Philosophy, Book VI, that being is divided into being per se and accidental being. Since being per se is in ten categories, there is no doubt among good interpreters that God is not included under this …
Because of this, we understand being in a sense such that God is above being, and is not under being, as Thomas teaches in the Commentaries on the Theological Sentences, Book 1.

warrants.t: Aristotle, Metaphysics VI, and Thomas on the Sentences, Book 1, as identified in the editors' notes.

judged.justification: Recruits Aquinas as the interpreter under whom Aristotle also puts God above being.

quotes.t: I shall add that some Platonists glory without justification, as if they had a mystery which was unknown to Aristotle, when they say
that there are two proper names of God, one and good, and thus good and one are prior to being. For as we showed, the Peripatetics know how God can be understood as above being.

open.t: 'Some Platonists' are not named; whether Ficino, Plotinus or Proclus is meant is not stated in the text.

judged.justification: A pointed remark that the Platonist claim to a mystery is answered inside Aristotelianism.
Supplies the Aristotelian counterpart to the Platonists' two names.

quotes.t: Let us now refute the arguments of the Platonists by which they contend that the one is superior to being. They hold this, not in the sense in which we also agree with it, but in an absolute sense, against …

judged.justification: Marks exactly what is conceded (a qualified one-above-being) and what is refused (an absolute one-above-being).
States that affirmation and denial of the divine names are reconciled by a rule, not by choosing a school.

open.t: This is one of two passages on angels in chapters 5 to 10; angelic knowledge is used only as an example of imperfection within a genus and no angelic order or hierarchy is described.

judged.justification: Shows that the treatise's only angelology is an example in an argument about divine names, not a doctrine of the angelic order.

quotes.t: But the life of the
angels is not perfect. Unless the vivifying ray of divine light constantly warmed it, it would all fall into nothingness.

open.t: The second of only two passages on angels in chapters 5 to 10; the chapter says nothing about angelic orders, the hierarchy of Dionysius or the Hebrew names.

judged.justification: Angelic being is described as contingent on a continuing divine illumination, in an argument about God's excluded imperfections.
Divine simplicity is used to exclude any reading of God as an aggregate of names, whether Platonist or Peripatetic.
Makes 'being itself' the result of subtraction, so being is not one name among others but what remains when all are stripped of particularity.
Being, one, good and truth are identified in God at the same level, by the same operation, undercutting the Platonist priority of one over being.
The chapter's structure is a graded negative theology, with the affirmations of ch. 4 as its early steps.
Even the formula 'God is above being, above one' is judged still a statement in the light, so the one-above-being thesis is itself transcended.
Places God above unity and existence alike, so neither the Platonist nor the Peripatetic ranking of one and being is final.

quotes.t: Dionysius the Areopagite saw this. After all that he wrote in the Symbolic Theology, in the Theological Institutions, in On the Divine Names, and in On Mystical Theology, he finally at the end of that work spoke as he could …

judged.justification: Pico reads Dionysius's Mystical Theology as the endpoint of the negative way, not as a claim that God is not being.

warrants.t: A quotation of the Latin text of De mystica theologia, which the editors identify in a note.
Plutarch and Varro, cited for the Egyptian view.

open.t: The Peripatetics who hold that God is body or soul of the heavens are not named in the text.

judged.justification: A named target inside the Aristotelian camp is missing; the polemic is not only aimed at Platonists.
Dionysius is placed before the Platonists as the source of the denial of intellect and life in God.
Here the one is prior to the many perfections, but as unity of perfection, not as a being-less principle.

warrants.t: Augustine, Sermon 340, identified in the editors' note.

open.t: 'Parisian theologians' are not identified individually; Aquinas is named elsewhere (ch. 4) but not here.

judged.justification: The scholastic doctrine is placed in agreement with the Platonists' denials through Augustine, a concord of schools rather than a choice.
An ineffable 'originative unity' is the positive sense the author gives the one that stands behind the names.

bears.note: A direct personal address to Poliziano in the middle of the argument.

judged.justification: The metaphysical argument is suspended for a claim that love reaches God where knowledge cannot; the treatise's subject is thus not finally cognitive.

bears.note: Addressed 'to you' at the point where the reconciliation is drawn.

judged.justification: Makes Republic VI's good-beyond-intellect and Aristotle's noesis noeseos two sides of one statement.

quotes.t: Consequently, if he knows himself, he is intellect and intelligible, for necessarily he who knows himself both knows and is known. Still, as I have said, if we understand these perfections as individual, or if, when we say intellect, we …

judged.justification: The negative theology closes on knowing by ignorance.
Anselm's formula is judged insufficient; the negative way overshoots it.
Pico presents his own solution as a key to reading Dionysius correctly against both underreading and invented mysticism.

warrants.t: From the functions Plato assigns to matter in the Timaeus: receptacle, nurse and nature.
Jamblichus, On the Pythagorean Sect, cited as a Platonist authority against the Platonists' claim that matter is one.

open.t: The translators' notes for this chapter do not identify the passage of Jamblichus.

judged.justification: One of the few named Platonists in the treatise; he is used against the school, not for it.

quotes.t: Further, prime matter is neither altogether without unity nor without being. Prime matter receives its precise unity from the same form from which it receives being. I pass over the dispute concerning the affirmative or negative unity of prime matter, …

open.t: The author declines to treat the dispute on the affirmative or negative unity of prime matter, calling it well known.

warrants.t: A reductio from the logic of genus and species: a higher genus can outrun the lower one.

judged.justification: Refutes the Platonists' universality claim by logic alone, which does not require Pico to settle what the Neoplatonic one is.

quotes.t: Two others were added to these four, namely, something and thing, by later followers of Avicenna. Avicenna interpolated the philosophy of Aristotle in many places, and because of this, Avicenna had a great war with Averroes. But as regards this …
These thinkers divide what is understood under one into one and something, which is not in disagreement with Plato, who in the Sophist enumerates something among these
most universal terms, and what is contained under being they divide into being and thing.

warrants.t: Avicenna, Metaphysics I, identified in the editors' note.

judged.justification: Ties each of the four to one of the causes, so the convertibility is a claim about the structure of createdness.
For creatures the order is being first and one after, the reverse of the Neoplatonic emanation; ch. 9 gives the order in God as cause.

quotes.t: Who does not see that these attributes are the same in extension? Give something being, and it is certainly also one. Who does not say one, says nothing, as Plato says in the Sophist.

judged.justification: The convertibility thesis stated in its shortest form, borrowed from Plato's own Sophist.

warrants.t: Augustine, Soliloquia II, identified in the editors' note.
Olympiodorus, In Phaedrum, identified in the editors' note.

judged.justification: A named Neoplatonist is corrected on the convertibility of good and being.

open.t: The author omits, as not the place to discuss everything, whether something is called good absolutely and being absolutely for the same reason.

judged.justification: Assigns each transcendental a divine attribute, giving unity a specific relational role.

open.t: The believers in two principles of good and evil are not named.

quotes.t: Let us examine once more how these are in God. They are not in God in relation to a cause that God does not have; for he, the cause of all things, is from nothing.

They can be considered in God in two ways, either as he consists absolutely in himself, or as he is the cause of other things. This distinction does not befit created things, as regards the present topic, since God is …

judged.justification: Distinguishes God as he is in himself from God as cause, and the ordering of the four differs between them.
In God as in himself, unity follows the plenitude of existence: one does not precede being here.
An identification of the four transcendentals with the Pythagorean tetraktys, offered tentatively.

quotes.t: If we were to assign these four names to God as he is the cause of things, the sequence must be reversed. First, he would be one, since he is understood in himself before he is understood as cause. Second, …
Because the cause that is called the end is prior to the exemplary, and the exemplary cause prior to the efficient cause
good pertains to the final cause, true to the exemplary cause, being to the efficient cause, then God, as he is cause, would have first the character of good, then of true, finally of being.
We touch briefly on all these points, which are still full of many and great questions.

open.t: In the same chapter God conceived in himself is first the plenitude of existence and then one, whereas in the reversed sequence one is first; the text says these points remain full of many and great questions and does not reconcile the two sequences.

judged.justification: In the order of God as cause the one comes first and being last, the reverse of the order for creatures.
States that the metaphysics is meant as a discipline of conduct.
The ontological triad of ch. 8-9 is directly converted into an ethic of imitation.

quotes.t: We are not one if we do not bind, by the union of virtue, sense bent downward with reason which looks at heavenly things. If there are two princes in us, reigning in turns, as it were, we for a …

judged.justification: Unity is given a moral definition as integration of sense and reason.
The convertibility thesis becomes a claim that moral failure is loss of being; the close of the treatise reads its metaphysics as a warning.

warrants.t: Miller infers Lorenzo's source from the tradition Ficino also followed.

open.t: Miller gives no evidence that Lorenzo drew on Ficino, only that the tradition was the same.

bears.note: Miller places Ficino in the tradition Lorenzo followed when he argued against Aristotle.
Lorenzo maintained the Platonic view in the discussion.

judged.justification: Gives the intellectual context: Lorenzo's Platonism, shared with Ficino, is the target position.

open.t: Miller's statement that Pico follows the Neoplatonic interpretation stands beside his account (below) that Pico argues the Parmenides is a dialectical exercise and denies an absolute one above being; how the two fit is not spelled out at this point.

judged.justification: Sets the Neoplatonic hierarchy as the framework Pico is said to accept.
Places Pico's reading of the Parmenides as early attention to the literary form of Plato's dialogues.

quotes.t: Ficino's interpretation had been influenced by the Neoplatonic emphasis on the first hypothesis of the dialogue. This first hypothesis describes the ineffable transcendence of the one, which is above and apart from all being and determination.

interpretation. which reads the opening hypothesis as a negative description of the one as a pure identity beyond relatedness, had gained added authority and plausibility from the commentary on the Parmenides written by the Neoplatonist Proclus. The commentary breaks off …

bears.note: Miller ties Ficino's reading of the Parmenides to Proclus's partial commentary, the reading Pico's ch. 2 opposes.

judged.justification: Explains the disagreement as a difference in which part of the Parmenides is treated as decisive.
A single line of transmission linking Proclus, Dionysius and Renaissance readers.

open.t: Miller does not name in this sentence the commentary he calls partial; the context points to the Proclus commentary described just before.

judged.justification: Names the target of Pico's exegetical polemic as a commentary tradition, not Plato.

quotes.t: (Ficino, in his commentary on the Parmenides, begun in the same year as Pico's On Being and the One, 1492, replies that Pico's interpretation is "against the opinion of all the Platonists."

warrants.t: Miller cites Ficino's commentary on the Parmenides in a note.

open.t: Miller quotes only six words of Ficino in translation and gives the reference as In Parmenidem II 1164; the Latin, its context and whether Ficino names Pico are not shown here.
Miller dates Pico's treatise to 1492 here but the volume's Biographical Note dates it 1491.

bears.note: Ficino's reply, as Miller reports it, rejects Pico's interpretation as against all the Platonists.

judged.justification: The only explicit statement in this source that Ficino answered Pico on the one; it dates and characterizes the quarrel.

quotes.t: For Ficino, following Plotinus and Proclus, Plato's dialectical form is only an outer covering for a profound metaphysical content.)

bears.note: States the Ficinian position that Pico's method-not-doctrine reading denies.

judged.justification: Formulates the hermeneutic disagreement: dialectic as covering versus dialectic as content.

quotes.t: Marsilio Ficino, the first Renaissance thinker to know all of the original writings of Plato, continued to interpret Plato within the framework of the Neoplatonic tradition, pagan and Christian, which Platonism had acquired during the previous thousand years
Although Pico's interpretation of Plato

differs in some respects from Ficino's, both Renaissance thinkers follow the long medieval tradition of the fundamental concord of the two Greek philosophers, transformed under the influence of Christianity.

open.t: Miller does not say in which respects Pico's interpretation differs from Ficino's beyond the Parmenides discussion.

bears.note: Miller sees Pico and Ficino as sharing concordism while differing in the reading of Plato.

judged.justification: Presents the quarrel as internal to a shared concordist tradition.

quotes.t: Being in the second sense means that which does not lack existence (esse). That which is (ens) means whatever participates existence. Pico is here utilizing the metaphysics of St. Thomas Aquinas, who was the first Christian philosopher to base his …

judged.justification: Identifies the Thomist source of the ens/esse distinction that carries the reconciliation.

quotes.t: There can be no doubt that Pico derived his metaphysic of existence from Thomas.

warrants.t: Miller supports this with the reports of Gian Francesco and the count of theses taken from Thomas.

open.t: Miller gives no reference for Gian Francesco's report.

bears.note: Gian Francesco is the source for Pico's near-agreement with Thomas.

open.t: Miller gives no source or list for the count of forty-five.

judged.justification: Formulates the key of the treatise: 'above being' means not one being among beings.
Miller, from outside the Renaissance frame, denies the historical premise of the concord that Pico proposes.

quotes.t: These two Greek philosophies can be made to coincide only when transformed into an altogether different philosophy: the highest principle in Plato turns out to be the same as the highest principle in Aristotle only because they are both identified …
Pico's concord of Plato and Aristotle, impossible within their philosophies taken on their own level, has been accomplished by transforming both into a different metaphysics.

judged.justification: States plainly that the concord is a product of Christian metaphysics, not a discovery about Plato and Aristotle.

warrants.t: Miller infers Proclus as Pico's reading source.

judged.justification: Explains the ethical close as the Neoplatonic return recast as grace.
Sets Pico's ethical unity against Plotinian union.

bears.note: Miller groups Pico with Ficino as co-Platonists reading the tradition constructively.

judged.justification: Frames the dispute as one between allies.

open.t: The Biographical Note dates On Being and the One to 1491 while the Introduction (l. 687) speaks of 1492 as the year of Pico's treatise and Ficino's commentary on the Parmenides; the volume does not reconcile them.

judged.justification: Tells the reader that the source identifications in the notes are Garin's, not independent.

bears.note: The editors call Poliziano an intimate friend of Ficino and of Pico.

open.t: The note says Pico used Ficino's translation for that passage; it does not say whether he used it throughout the treatise.

bears.note: Pico's own quotation of the Parmenides that anchors his dialectic-exercise argument comes through Ficino's Latin.

judged.justification: Pico's polemic against the Neoplatonic Parmenides rests on Ficino's own Latin text of the dialogue.

open.t: The note cites Plotinus for the claim about the first hypothesis; the text of the treatise does not itself name Plotinus.
The editors do not identify the Psalm reference for the verse quoted according to the Hebrew text.
No note in this chapter identifies the Jamblichus passage that Pico cites.
The note only compares Helias Cretensis's Quaestio de ente, essentia et uno; it does not say Pico used it.

judged.justification: Points to a scholastic quaestio on the same topic as a comparison.
